question: Brain freeze starts when something icy touches one particular part of your mouth, and pressing your warm tongue against that spot helps stop it. Which part?
source_excerpt: pain signals from the roof of the mouth as coming from the forehead

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has had brain freeze and assumes the cold reaches the brain itself. In fact the trigger is a specific spot in the mouth, and the cure is something you can do instantly without stopping the car.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources say cold on the palate (roof of the mouth) triggers brain freeze and that pressing the tongue to it relieves it; no newer findings contradict this (https://www.popsci.com/science/what-is-brain-freeze/).

explanation: The cold hits the blood vessels in your palate, and the nerves there send a pain signal your brain wrongly places in your forehead. Your warm tongue heats the spot back up and calms the reaction.

question: A chili's burn keeps mammals from eating its seeds, but one whole group of animals feels no burn at all and happily spreads the seeds far and wide. Which animals?
source_excerpt: the chicken version of the capsaicin receptor does not respond to capsaicin, while the rat version does

extra.why_interesting: People assume chili heat is a defence against every animal. It is actually selective: it deters mammals, whose teeth crush the seeds, while recruiting the one group that flies the seeds far away unharmed. Players can reason toward it from 'who eats berries and spreads seeds?'
extra.verification_notes: Birds' TRPV1 doesn't respond to capsaicin, so they eat chilies and disperse viable seeds while mammals are deterred (Jordt & Julius 2002; Tewksbury & Nabhan 2001).

explanation: Birds' heat sensors don't respond to capsaicin, so to them a hot chili is just a tasty berry. The seeds pass through them undamaged, which is why some bird seed is spiked with chili to keep squirrels away.
